newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Indians defiant as eviction deadline passes.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Indians defiant as eviction deadline passes.

text.p: More than 200 Guarani-Kaiowa Indians on Friday donned war paint and remained defiantly on disputed land in western Brazil although a deadline for them to clear out has come and gone, a lawyer said.
"The Indians are there, wearing paint and ready to fight to the death to stay," Maucir Paulette, a lawyer for the Catholic Church's Indian Missionary Council (CIMI), told Reuters.
The Indians were given until Wednesday to obey a court order to abandon their village and three ancient cemeteries, which lie inside a private cattle ranch in the western state of Mato Grosso do Sul.
But the Guarani-Kaiowa stayed put, waiting for a court to rule on their appeal of the order, as pressure built to forcefully evict them from the land they consider sacred.
"Ranchers are threatening to enter to throw out the Indians but if they do that it will be a disaster," Paulette said.
He said federal and state courts, uncertain who has jurisdiction over the case, have been shuffling the appeal back and forth without issuing a ruling. "No one wants to make a decision," he added.
Court officials could not be reached for comment late on Friday.

The Guarani-Kaiowas, who were joined by about 70 nearby villagers to beat back any attempt by police to clear the land, have threatened to fight to the death or commit suicide rather than leave the land.
The Indians were armed with guns, clubs, bows and arrows. They also stockpiled about 15 gallons (60 liters) of gasoline for firebombs or to set fire to themselves, Paulette has said.

A court official said last week the judge who ordered the Indians out was merely following the decision of a more senior tribunal, which upheld a decision on a landowner appeal of the areas demarcation as a reservation.
Before European colonisation, the Guaranis and Kaiowas were flourishing tribes who roamed a vast region of Brazil and part of what is now Paraguay.
As settlers penetrated deeper into Brazil's interior, the groups were pushed ever more remote regions. Today they live in poverty in small areas surrounded by huge farms.
